properties.title: ADR-0017: Console topology & session ownership (multi-zone BFF over openid-client + Redis)

pages.content:
**Status** — proposed
**Date** — 2026-08-13

**Context**

The frontend tier of `paigasus-core` has never been scoped: <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/368830e8fbaa8101b0ffded7a3de3b53">Polyglot Monorepo Scoping</mention-page> deferred it explicitly (*"Frontend architecture beyond 'Next.js console exists' — needs its own design"*), and `ts/apps/paigasus-console` is a bare App Router skeleton. Two backend services now exist (`paigasus-iam`, `paigasus-gateway`) and each needs an operator-facing surface. Full design: <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3bb830e8fbaa8188adf2c6bfebf67ed5">Frontend Architecture Scoping</mention-page>.

The binding constraint comes from <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/395830e8fbaa8172b5bcd743d81c0bc0">ADR-0015: Authenticator port & OIDC strategy (BYO-IdP, delegated authentication)</mention-page>: **IAM is a pure resource server.** It validates externally-issued access tokens, performs no authorization-code flow, stores no passwords, and has no concept of a session. Whatever runs the login flow therefore lives entirely outside IAM, and the frontend tier is the only candidate.

Three further inputs shaped the choice. The deploy target is **self-hosted OCI containers**, so no hosting-specific features and no build-time configuration — a single image must serve customers with different IdP issuers. The audiences **overlap but are distinct** (org admins vs. developers using the gateway), so shared login is desirable but no app may depend on another being up to authenticate someone. And the stated drivers for multiple apps were **independent deploy cadence** and **domain separation**.

**Decision**

1. **Multi-zone topology.** One Next.js app per backend service, each its own image and its own deploy pipeline, path-routed behind a **single origin** (`/iam/*`, `/gateway/*`). Each app sets `basePath` + `assetPrefix` so static chunks never collide.
2. **Backend-for-frontend.** The browser never holds a token. The session cookie carries an **opaque session id only** — `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Path=/`, host-only on the single origin, so all zones read the same cookie.
3. **Session state lives in Redis**, keyed by session id: access token, refresh token, expiry, principal PRN, and the memberships/role-grants snapshot from `Introspect`. An in-memory adapter sits behind the same port for dev and single-node self-hosting.
4. **`openid-client` v6 is the relying-party library.** Protocol handling — PKCE, state, nonce, discovery, JWKS, token exchange and verification — stays in a conformant library; the ~200 lines of session glue around it are ours.
5. **Auth routes are embedded in every app** via a shared route-handler factory, not centralized in one app. **One OIDC client registration** with one redirect URI per zone.
6. **Token refresh is single-flight** under a per-session Redis lock.
7. **Middleware performs cookie-presence checks and redirect-to-login only.** Session resolution happens in server components and route handlers via `getSession()`.
8. **`can()` is cosmetic.** It reads role grants from the session to hide affordances. IAM's Cedar evaluation is authoritative, and the UI must render the resulting 403 correctly.

**Consequences**

- **The single origin is what makes the shared session cheap.** One cookie across all zones, no cross-domain SSO dance, and no CORS configuration on any Rust service. This is the main reason multi-zone beat separate origins.
- **Ingress path-routing becomes part of the deployment contract.** A self-hoster's ingress is no longer incidental configuration — it is how the product is assembled. Helm must render the ingress rules and the console's zone map from one values block so they cannot drift.
- **Cross-zone navigation is a hard navigation.** A `<Link>` to another zone attempts a client-side RSC prefetch against a route its own server does not have, and fails. A `<ZoneLink>` abstraction is mandatory, and the failure mode — an intermittently broken nav item — is invisible to unit tests.
- **Redis becomes a login-path dependency.** Mitigated by the in-memory adapter and the existing circuit breaker (SMA-476) and retry budget (SMA-473), but it is a real new coupling on an availability-critical path.
- **All zones share the session cookie and therefore the cookie/crypto secret.** That is an operational coupling: one secret mounted into every console image.
- **Real logout and revocation become possible.** Server-side session state can be invalidated; a self-contained encrypted cookie cannot. For a product shipping Cedar policies and a partitioned audit log, this is a requirement rather than a nicety.
- **We own the session code and therefore its tests.** The protocol is the library's; cookie flags, session fixation, refresh-rotation races, and logout semantics are ours to get right and to keep right.
- **Adding a third service costs one app and one redirect URI**, not a new IdP client registration. The self-hoster's IdP configuration burden stays at one client regardless of how many zones exist.
- **No app is a login SPOF for another.** The price is that the same auth route factory is mounted in every image — one implementation, N mounts.
- **A self-hoster with no IdP still cannot log in.** IAM requires an OIDC issuer, and this decision does not change that. An optional bundled IdP (Better Auth's `oauth-provider` plugin issues JWTs with JWKS and introspection, which IAM's RS256/ES256 validator already consumes) would slot in as just another configured issuer. Deliberately deferred until a self-hoster asks.

**Alternatives considered**

- **Separate origins per app** (`iam.paigasus.io`, `gateway.paigasus.io`) with cross-app SSO via an IdP `prompt=none` redirect. The strongest domain separation, and it enables per-tenant vanity domains. Rejected on the self-hoster tax: **two OIDC client registrations per customer**, each of which someone's IdP admin must create, plus a cert and DNS entry per app and a redirect round-trip on first hit of each zone. Not foreclosed — it is the natural upgrade if per-tenant domains ever become a product requirement.
- **A single app with route groups** (`(iam)`, `(gateway)`). Simplest by a wide margin — one image, one session, soft navigation throughout — and genuinely defensible for a stateless console, where "redeploy everything" is a short rolling update. Rejected because it drops the independent-deploy-cadence driver outright and lets one bad page red the whole build. Note this choice is **cheap to reverse in either direction** provided the package boundaries are drawn correctly, so the app count is not the expensive part of this ADR.
- **Better Auth with a primary database.** Batteries-included, well-reviewed, and its `organization`, `apiKey` and `admin` plugins cover real ground. Rejected: it requires a TS ORM and a second migration system in a repo whose entire persistence story is Rust SeaORM migrations, and its `user`/`account` tables duplicate what IAM already owns — IAM JIT-provisions a `User` from `(issuer, subject)` and audit-logs it through the outbox, so a second user table would hold identity state invisible to the audit log. Its `organization` plugin, the library's biggest draw, directly competes with IAM M1 tenancy and M3 Cedar roles and would have to be refused by convention.
- **Better Auth in database-less mode.** Verified against current source: without `options.database` it falls back to a memory adapter and auto-enables `account.storeAccountCookie`. Its own source comment is explicit — *"secondaryStorage holds sessions and verification, not account records, so without a primary database the account (and its OAuth tokens) only has a durable home in a cookie."* Rejected because that re-opens every failure mode Decision 3 exists to prevent: no server-side revocation, the 4 KB cookie budget against a full grant set, and — worst under multi-zone — two zones racing a rotating refresh token with no shared lock.
- **Auth.js / NextAuth.** Rejected for the same identity-model reasons as Better Auth, and because it models an *identity* session where what is needed is raw custody of an access token carrying the right `aud` for IAM. Note the objection is **not** module-scope configuration: in a Node container module scope evaluates at server boot, which is runtime. The genuine build-time hazards are narrower — `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` inlining and config validation running during `next build` prerender.
- **SPA with tokens in the browser** (PKCE in the browser, tokens in memory, no BFF). Simplest infrastructure — no Redis, no server session. Rejected: tokens become reachable from JavaScript, server components cannot fetch data, and every deployment-varying value would have to reach the browser, which `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` inlining makes impossible for a single self-hosted image.

properties.title: ADR-0018: Connect-ES over gRPC for the console↔service transport; no OpenAPI surface

pages.content:
**Status** — proposed
**Date** — 2026-08-13

**Context**

`paigasus-iam` exposes two API surfaces. The **REST** surface (`/v1/organizations`, `/v1/teams`, `/v1/authz/*`, …) is built from **hand-written serde DTOs** (`adapters::http::dto`), with no OpenAPI document and no `utoipa`/`aide` in the dependency tree. The **gRPC** surface is generated from `contracts/` per <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/368830e8fbaa81a99777ceb7421b64d7">ADR-0004: Protobuf + buf as the single source of truth for wire contracts</mention-page>. So one surface is contract-derived and gated, the other is hand-maintained on both ends.

Three facts made the choice tractable. `contracts/buf.gen.yaml` **already** runs `buf.build/bufbuild/es:v2.13.0` into `ts/packages/paigasus-proto/src/generated`. The gateway **already** dials IAM over gRPC — `adapters/iam/client.rs` is a tonic `Channel` (h2c in-cluster, TLS optional, `connect_lazy`) shared by `AuthnServiceClient` and `AuthorizationServiceClient`. And <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3bb830e8fbaa8188adf2c6bfebf67ed5">ADR-0017</mention-page> puts a BFF between browser and services, which means **the console's API client runs in Node, not in a browser** — removing the constraint that normally forces grpc-web on a web frontend.

<mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/368830e8fbaa8101b0ffded7a3de3b53">Polyglot Monorepo Scoping</mention-page> § 2 already anticipated this path: *"Connect protocol speaks both gRPC and Connect-over-HTTP, so a TS client can talk to a tonic Rust server without Envoy in front."*

**Decision**

1. **The console calls IAM over gRPC using Connect-ES**, via `createClient(Service, transport)` over `createGrpcTransport` from `@connectrpc/connect-node` — **server-side only**, inside the BFF.
2. **No grpc-web, no `tonic-web`, no Envoy.** The BFF eliminates the browser-can't-speak-gRPC problem rather than working around it.
3. **No codegen change.** Connect-ES v2 dropped its separate generator plugin; protobuf-es v2 emits service descriptors itself. `buf.gen.yaml` is untouched and the existing codegen-drift gate keeps protecting the output. The cost is two catalog entries.
4. **We will not add `utoipa`/`aide` or publish an OpenAPI document** for the console's benefit.
5. **HTTP-only surfaces get a small hand-written fetch client** in `@paigasus/sdk/http`: `/v1/users`, `/v1/outbox/dead-letters/*`, `/v1/authz/system-policies/{id}/retire`, and the gateway's OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint.
6. **Transports are cached per base URL; authorization is attached per call** via an interceptor reading the request-scoped session. No token ever lives in a cached object.
7. **`@paigasus/sdk` is server-only**, enforced by `import 'server-only'` at its entry point.

**Consequences**

- **Console types come from the contract source of truth** and are already protected by the codegen-drift gate. There is no hand-maintained TypeScript DTO layer to drift against the Rust one — which is what would have happened had the console consumed the REST surface.
- **`ci/affected-graph/run.sh` will fail the moment `@paigasus/sdk` depends on `@paigasus/proto`.** The `contracts->proto` case asserts the affected set *equals* `contracts,paigasus-proto-rs,paigasus-proto-py,paigasus-proto-ts,paigasus-gateway-rs,paigasus-iam-rs`, and strict equality fails on any extra project. The expected set must gain `paigasus-sdk-ts` and every app downstream of it, in the same change. This is the known kernel gotcha generalized to TypeScript.
- **The hand-written HTTP slice is the drift risk this ADR does not eliminate.** It shrinks toward just the gateway as protos are added for the three IAM ops endpoints — which per ADR-0004 arguably belong in the contract regardless.
- **The console requires HTTP/2 to IAM.** In-cluster h2c matches the gateway's existing channel setup, so this introduces no new transport posture; but a deployment that terminates HTTP/1.1 in front of IAM would break the console while leaving the REST surface working.
- **Authorization propagation is mandatory, not optional.** The M2 tower middleware wraps *both* transports, so gRPC enforces bearer tokens exactly as HTTP does.
- **The REST surface keeps no first-party generated client.** It remains the external/customer-facing surface. If it is ever published as a *supported* API, the OpenAPI question returns — and should be answered then, for that reason, rather than pre-emptively here.
- **The gateway's chat endpoint stays HTTP + SSE deliberately.** It is OpenAI-compatible by design; forcing it into proto would break the SDK compatibility that is the point of the surface.
- **Any future browser-direct call needs a separate decision.** This ADR deliberately does not enable one — no grpc-web transport is configured and no service is exposed to the browser.

**Alternatives considered**

- **`utoipa`/`aide` → `openapi.json` → generated TS client + drift gate.** Produces a genuinely useful artifact and would put the REST surface under a generated-client discipline matching the gRPC one. Rejected on cost/benefit for *this* use: annotating roughly 40 axum handlers and maintaining those annotations indefinitely, to reach a place the proto path already occupies for free. The decision flips the day the REST API becomes a published, supported customer surface.
- **Hand-written TypeScript REST client.** Fastest to a first screen and zero backend work. Rejected: the REST DTOs are hand-written on the Rust side too, so both ends would drift independently with no gate anywhere in between.
- **`tonic-web` + `@connectrpc/connect-web` in the browser.** The conventional answer for a web frontend calling a gRPC backend. Rejected as unnecessary under ADR-0017 — it would add a translation layer, expose services directly to browsers, and require CORS, all to solve a problem the BFF already removes.
- **Direct browser→service calls with CORS.** Rejected for the same reasons plus the token-custody consequences settled in ADR-0017.

properties.title: ADR-0019: Canonical error model — google.rpc.ErrorInfo across HTTP, gRPC and the OpenAI envelope

pages.content:
**Status** — proposed
**Date** — 2026-08-13

**Context**

`paigasus-core` has four client-facing error surfaces, and a real error vocabulary exists on exactly one of them.

- **IAM HTTP** is good: `TenancyError::code()` yields stable kebab codes (`slug-conflict`, `parent-archived`, `nothing-to-rename`), `ErrorClass` maps to status, the body is `{"error":{"code","message"}}`, and `Internal` never leaks its source.
- **IAM gRPC** has no structured detail at all. `status_to_grpc` stuffs the code in-band: `Status::new(code, format!("{}: {}", e.code(), e))`. The code comment is candid about why — *"tonic has no structured-error-detail convention by default."*
- **IAM authn gRPC** carries no machine-readable code whatsoever; `authn_status` returns static strings (`"invalid bearer token"`).
- **The gateway** uses the OpenAI-compatible envelope `{message, type, param, code}`, which is a **binding external compatibility contract** — OpenAI client SDKs branch on `error.type`.

The practical consequence: a gRPC client can recover an error code only by splitting the message on `": "`. With a console now consuming that surface (<mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3bb830e8fbaa8188adf2c6bfebf67ed5">ADR-0018</mention-page>), that fragility becomes load-bearing.

<mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/368830e8fbaa8101b0ffded7a3de3b53">Polyglot Monorepo Scoping</mention-page> planned for this and it was never built: its proto layout lists `common/v1/errors.proto # canonical error envelope`, and its kernel scope includes *"Canonical error types (the typed errors that wire-format into `paigasus.common.v1.Error`)"*.

**Decision**

1. **The code is the contract; the envelope is per-surface.** All four envelopes stay exactly as they are. One vocabulary underneath them.
2. **Error identity is `(domain, reason)`, expressed as `google.rpc.ErrorInfo`** — `domain: "iam.paigasus.io"`, `reason: "slug-conflict"`, plus a `metadata` map. Adopting an existing standard rather than inventing an envelope.
3. **Kebab-case `reason` is retained** — a deliberate, documented deviation from Google's UPPER_SNAKE convention, because the existing codes are already a tested contract and renaming them is churn for aesthetics.
4. **gRPC carries `ErrorInfo` in the `grpc-status-details-bin` trailer** via `tonic-types`' `ErrorDetails`. The in-band `"{code}: {message}"` prefix is removed; the message becomes purely human-readable.
5. **The authn funnel keeps its separate status mapping and its static, non-revealing messages**, and gains machine codes.
6. **Every error carries a correlation/trace id.** Internal errors return a generic message plus the id; detail stays in logs.
7. **Retryability is data, not inference** — a `retryable` entry in `metadata`, so clients never hard-code "503 means retry."
8. **The registry lives in `contracts/proto/paigasus/common/v1/error.proto`** as doc-commented string constants — the `errors.proto` the scoping document planned — guarded by a **two-way drift gate**: every code Rust *emits* is in the registry, and every code a client *consumes* is too.
9. **Consumers branch on `(domain, reason)` only, never on message text.** An unknown reason falls back to a generic presentation plus the correlation id.

**Consequences**

- **The gateway is an in-repo consumer of IAM's gRPC status and must change in the same commit.** It holds `IamError::Rpc(tonic::Status)` specifically so its auth middleware can branch on it; removing the in-band code prefix changes what that branching sees.
- **Removing the in-band prefix is a wire-visible change** to the gRPC message format. It is free today because there are no external consumers, and expensive the moment there are. That timing is the main argument for doing this now rather than later.
- **`domain` disambiguates without renaming.** A bare `internal` from IAM and from the gateway are distinguishable in a console toast and in logs, while every existing kebab code string survives untouched. This is why `ErrorInfo` beat the obvious alternative of dotted namespaces like `iam.tenancy.slug-conflict`.
- **buf's breaking-change detection does not protect string constants**, so the registry is guarded by the drift gate rather than by the proto gate. The gate must check **both** directions — `:observability-drift` only checks that names resolve, which is exactly how a metric's prose drifted across three unlinked places. Here the same trap spans the code, the Rust message, and the UI copy.
- **The OpenAI envelope is preserved intact.** The gateway's `type` keeps its OpenAI semantics for SDK compatibility; the canonical reason rides in `code`. No caller of the chat surface sees a change.
- **Distinct authn codes leak nothing new.** The authn messages are already distinct per case, so attaching codes adds no information a caller cannot already infer — while the uniform, non-revealing message posture is preserved.
- **Every error construction site gains a domain and a correlation id.** That is real, if mechanical, churn across IAM and the gateway, and it slightly widens the log and audit surface.
- **The kernel is the natural long-term home for the canonical error types**, per the scoping document's own kernel criteria. This ADR does not move them there; it defines the wire contract first.
- **A user-reportable correlation id is the single highest-value item here** for a self-hosted product: without it, supporting a deployment you cannot access is guesswork.

**Alternatives considered**

- **Invent a bespoke Paigasus error envelope** shared by all surfaces. Rejected: a contract we would have to design, document and defend, for no gain over a standard that already models exactly `(domain, reason, metadata)` and that gRPC tooling already transports.
- **Unify all four envelopes on one shape.** Superficially the cleanest reading of "uniform." Rejected outright: the gateway's OpenAI-compatible envelope is the *product* — SDK compatibility is why callers can point an OpenAI client at it — and unifying it away would break every consumer.
- **Keep the in-band `"code: message"` string** and have clients split on `": "`. Zero backend work. Rejected: it forces string parsing into every consumer, breaks the moment a message legitimately contains `": "`, and makes the code inseparable from human-facing text that should be free to change or be localized.
- **A proto enum for error codes** instead of strings. Would bring the vocabulary under buf's breaking-change gate. Rejected for forward-compatibility: a new code in one service would force a bindings regeneration everywhere, and an older client receiving a newer enum value gets an opaque number rather than a name it can log. The registry plus drift gate buys the protection without the coupling.
- **Status quo.** Rejected: it makes the console's error handling depend on parsing a human-readable string, and leaves the authn surface with no machine-readable codes at all.

properties.title: ADR-0020: Service capability discovery — addresses from config, capabilities from the service

pages.content:
**Status** — proposed
**Date** — 2026-08-13

**Context**

`paigasus-core` is self-hostable, and a given deployment may run IAM alone, IAM plus the gateway, or more services later. A console that hard-codes which services exist would be wrong in most deployments; one that hard-codes which *features* each service has would be wrong after any partial upgrade, since self-hosters upgrade components independently.

Three properties need distinguishing, and they cannot share a mechanism:

- **Configured** — the operator deployed this service and supplied its address. Only the deployment knows this.
- **Reachable** — it is answering right now.
- **Capable** — which features that particular version supports.

There is no service registry in this architecture: Kubernetes DNS plus Helm values *are* the registry. Nothing is discoverable without an address. `iam.proto` already carries a stub for the other half — `ServiceInfo { string prn }`, commented as a placeholder that "carries a service PRN string for now." Full design: <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3bb830e8fbaa8188adf2c6bfebf67ed5">Frontend Architecture Scoping</mention-page> § 3.

**Decision**

1. **Addresses come from deployment configuration** (Helm values → environment), never from discovery.
2. **Capabilities come from the service itself.** `ServiceInfo` grows in `common/v1` into a descriptor: service name, version, and a list of capability keys (`iam.authz.cedar`, `iam.apikeys`, `iam.audit`, `gateway.chat.stream`).
3. **Capability keys are strings, append-only**, with the registry maintained as a doc comment in the proto.
4. **Discovery is lazy and request-scoped**, performed in an authenticated user's context and cached in Redis (`svcinfo:<service>`, ~60 s TTL, stale-while-revalidate, single-flight). **No boot-time probe and no service credential.**
5. **Three UI states, not two:** absent from config → not rendered at all; configured and answering → normal; configured but unreachable → **rendered disabled with a reason, never hidden**.
6. **Version-skew contract:** clients support **N-1 minor** of each service. An unknown capability key is ignored; an absent capability means the feature is off; a client must never *require* a capability released in the same version as itself.
7. **Helm renders the ingress rule and the console's zone/service configuration from one values block**, so the two cannot drift.

**Consequences**

- **No unauthenticated capability endpoint and no provisioned service-account credential.** Running discovery inside a user request sidesteps both — there is no boot-time context in which the console holds a credential, and adding one would mean every self-hoster provisions a service account before the console works. The cost is that nothing is known before login, which is acceptable because the login page has no navigation.
- **The descriptor becomes part of every service's contract.** A new Paigasus service is not consumable by the console until it implements it. That is a deliberate, small tax on service authors.
- **Capability gating is cosmetic, exactly like `can()`.** The server remains authoritative and must handle an unimplemented call gracefully; a client that treated the capability list as a security boundary would be wrong.
- **A stale cache can advertise a capability for up to the TTL after a downgrade.** Acceptable: the failure mode is one rejected call with a clean error, not a security issue.
- **Strings mean buf's breaking-change gate does not guard the key vocabulary.** The registry plus a drift gate does — the same posture <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3bb830e8fbaa8188adf2c6bfebf67ed5">ADR-0019</mention-page> takes for error codes, and for the same forward-compatibility reason.
- **"Degraded" must be a first-class state or the ops signal is destroyed.** Hiding a deployed-but-unreachable service tells the operator their deployment succeeded when it did not. This is the single most important line in this ADR, and the state most likely to be implemented wrong — it needs its own test.
- **Discovery adds a Redis read on the first authenticated request** per service per TTL. Redis is already on the login path from <mention-page url="https://app.notion.com/p/3bb830e8fbaa8188adf2c6bfebf67ed5">ADR-0017</mention-page>, so this introduces no new dependency.
- **The N-1 rule constrains feature rollout.** A console feature depending on a brand-new service capability must ship at least one release after that capability, or self-hosters on a lagging service see a broken affordance.

**Alternatives considered**

- **Static configuration declaring capabilities as well as addresses.** Simplest and fully deterministic, with no runtime probe and no failure mode. Rejected: it makes the operator responsible for keeping a capability list in sync with the versions they actually deployed — a duplication that is silently wrong after every partial upgrade, and precisely the version-skew bug this ADR exists to prevent.
- **Full discovery, including addresses**, via a service registry (Consul, etcd) or the Kubernetes API. Rejected: it introduces a substantial new infrastructure dependency into a product that must be self-hostable without one, and Helm values already carry the deployment truth faithfully.
- **Hard-coding capabilities in the console per release**, pinned to a known service version. Rejected: it forces lockstep upgrades of console and services, which is precisely the coupling multi-zone deployment exists to avoid.
- **Probing at boot with a dedicated service account.** Gives a warm cache and lets the console report topology before anyone logs in. Rejected on the provisioning burden: every self-hoster would have to create a service account and API key before the console starts, to gain something only visible on a page that has no navigation anyway.
- **Hiding unreachable services.** Simpler UI with fewer states. Rejected: it converts an outage into an apparent configuration change, which is the worst possible presentation for an operator.

properties.title: ADR-0021: Tailwind + Radix primitives (shadcn-style) over a component library for @paigasus/ui

pages.content:
**Status** — proposed
**Date** — 2026-08-13

**Context**

`ts/packages/paigasus-ui` is scaffolded with a React peer dependency and an empty `src/index.ts`. It needs a foundation before any console surface is built.

The surfaces it must serve are operator and admin UI: tenancy trees (org → team → project), Cedar policy editing, role-grant and membership management, API-key issuance, audit-log tables, and dead-letter queue inspection with replay. That workload is dense, table-heavy, and full of a11y-critical interactive primitives — menus, dialogs, comboboxes, tooltips. It is not a marketing surface.

Two repo-level constraints matter. `paigasus-core` is public and Apache-2.0, so dependency licensing and long-term maintainability are visible to everyone. And the product is self-hosted and expected to be brandable, so the theming model must be ours rather than a vendor's.

**Decision**

1. **Tailwind v4 (CSS-first configuration) plus Radix primitives**, with shadcn-style **copy-in components owned in the repo** rather than a runtime component dependency.
2. **Design tokens as CSS custom properties**, with light/dark handled entirely through token redefinition.
3. **`@paigasus/ui` never imports from `next/*`** and stays framework-agnostic React. Navigation is injected — components accept a link component or read one from context.
4. **Tailwind v4's `@source` must cover the package's `src`**, or the app build tree-shakes the package's classes away.
5. **Radix owns the a11y-critical primitives.** Hand-rolled menus, dialogs and comboboxes are explicitly out of scope.

**Consequences**

- **No runtime dependency on a vendor's design decisions.** Restyling to a brand is configuration of our own tokens rather than fighting a theme system, which matters for a self-hosted product customers may want to skin.
- **We own the components, including their upgrades.** Copy-in means no automatic upstream bug fixes or a11y improvements; pulling an improvement is a manual merge. This is the real cost of the approach and it compounds with the number of components vendored.
- **The `@source` requirement is a genuine footgun.** Forget it and the package's classes vanish — typically only in a production build, where the failure looks like broken styling rather than a build error. Worth a smoke test.
- **`@paigasus/ui` tests in jsdom with no Next runtime**, which is the direct payoff of rule 3 and keeps the fastest test tier fast.
- **The shadcn CLI assumes an application, not a shared workspace package.** Its monorepo mode and workspace aliases need configuring once, and the generated import paths need checking against the package's own exports.
- **Slower to a first working admin screen** than a batteries-included library — there is no pre-built data grid, date picker, or form layout. For dense table surfaces specifically, this is where the cost is felt most.
- **a11y remains our responsibility even with Radix.** Radix covers keyboard and ARIA semantics for the primitives it provides; composition, focus order, labelling and contrast are still ours. `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` is already configured, and axe assertions in component tests are the intended backstop.

**Alternatives considered**

- **A full component library (MUI, Mantine, Chakra).** Fastest path to a working admin UI, with data grids and form layouts included — genuinely attractive for exactly the table-heavy surfaces listed above. Rejected: the theming model comes with it, restyling to a brand is fought rather than configured, and the bundle and upgrade cadence are the vendor's. For a product where the console is a long-lived operator surface rather than a one-off internal tool, owning the layer is worth the slower start.
- **Tailwind only, hand-rolled components.** Smallest dependency surface, maximum control. Rejected: it puts menus, dialogs, comboboxes and focus management in our hands, which is precisely where hand-rolled a11y goes wrong and where the defects are hardest to notice without assistive-technology testing.
- **Headless UI instead of Radix.** Comparable philosophy and a smaller surface. Rejected on breadth: Radix covers more of the primitives this console needs, and shadcn's component set — the thing being copied in — is built against Radix, so choosing otherwise means porting each component.
- **No shared UI package; each app owns its components.** Fewer moving parts while there is only one app. Rejected: it guarantees divergence in exactly the elements users read as "one product" (header, nav, tables, empty states), and the multi-zone topology of ADR-0017 makes visual consistency across hard navigations more important, not less.
